pages.text: To get I from P = I²R, undo × R first (2300 ÷ 23 = 100), then the square. For a positive amount like a current, a [[square root]] undoes a square, so √100 = 10.

pages.name: Find the current
pages.task: A 4 Ω resistor gives out 144 W. Using P = I²R, what current does it carry?
pages.why: Undo × R first, 144 ÷ 4 = 36, so I² = 36. Then undo the square, √36 = 6 A, since 6 × 6 = 36. As a check, 6² × 4 = 144.

pages.name: Two square roots
pages.text: Squaring both sides of I = √100 gives I² = 100. But −10 × −10 = 100 too, so −10 sneaks in. It fails I = √100, as √ means the positive root.

pages.name: Make p₂ the subject
pages.task: In p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, which formula gives the new pressure p₂?
pages.why: p₂ is multiplied by V₂, so divide both sides by V₂. p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂, which here is 4 × 9 ÷ 3 = 12 bar. As a check, 4 × 9 = 12 × 3.

pages.task: Gas fills 10 L at a gauge reading of 2 bar. Squeezed at a steady temperature until the gauge reads 5 bar, about what volume does it fill?
pages.why: Add about 1 bar for the atmosphere, so 3 bar and 6 bar absolute. Then V₂ = 3 × 10 ÷ 6 = 5 L. As a check, 3 × 10 = 6 × 5.

pages.name: How long a run?
pages.task: A cable's table value is 12 mV/A/m, as an example. At 25 A, how long can the run be if you allow, say, a 6 V drop?
pages.why: Each metre drops 12 × 25 = 300 mV. A 6 V drop is 6000 mV, so 6000 ÷ 300 = 20 m. As a check, 12 × 25 × 20 ÷ 1000 = 6.

pages.name: Make R the subject
pages.task: In P = I²R, which formula gives the resistance R?
pages.why: R is multiplied by I², so divide both sides by I². R = P ÷ I², which here is 500 ÷ 25 = 20 Ω. As a check, 5² × 20 = 500.
